**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I sit here, staring at the blank page, the cursor blinking like a metronome counting down the seconds of my indecision. A thousand words—what a strange, arbitrary number. A thousand steps could take you nowhere if you’re walking in circles. A thousand dollars might buy you freedom or just another month’s rent. A thousand words could be a manifesto, a confession, a eulogy, or just the ramblings of a mind too tired to sleep.

I think about the things that haunt me. Not ghosts, not in the way you’d expect—no sheet-draped specters or chains rattling in the dark. My ghosts are quieter. They’re the conversations I didn’t have, the letters I never sent, the doors I walked away from without looking back. They’re the version of myself I thought I’d be by now, the one who had it all figured out, who didn’t flinch at the sound of their own voice.

There’s a coffee stain on my desk, shaped like a question mark. I don’t remember spilling it. Maybe it’s been there for weeks, slowly darkening into the wood, becoming a permanent part of the landscape. That’s how regret works, isn’t it? It seeps in unnoticed, and by the time you realize it’s there, it’s already stained everything.

I used to believe in grand narratives. The hero’s journey, the redemption arc, the moment of clarity that changes everything. But life isn’t a story with a three-act structure. It’s more like a collection of short vignettes, some funny, some tragic, most forgettable. The man who cut in line at the grocery store. The way the light hits the pavement after rain. The time you laughed so hard you cried, and for a second, nothing else mattered.

I wonder if we’re all just trying to distract ourselves from the fact that we’re hurtling through space on a rock, with no real instruction manual. We build routines, relationships, careers—scaffolding to keep the void at bay. And yet, the void is always there, humming quietly in the background, like the refrigerator you only notice when it turns off.

Sometimes, I envy people who believe in something unshakable. Faith, fate, the inherent goodness of humanity. I want to believe those things, but belief has always felt like a muscle I never quite developed. Instead, I have questions. So many questions. Why do we love the people we love? Why does time feel like it’s accelerating? Why is it so hard to say what we mean?

I think about the last time I was truly present. Not scrolling, not planning, not replaying past mistakes in my head. Just *there*. It was years ago, sitting on a beach at dusk, the sky bleeding into the ocean. A stranger’s dog ran up to me, dropped a stick at my feet, and waited. I threw it. The dog brought it back. We did this for twenty minutes, no words exchanged, just the rhythm of the game, the sound of waves, the way the world narrowed to that single, stupid, perfect moment.

I wish I could bottle that feeling. The absence of want. The quiet joy of being an animal in the sun, unburdened by the weight of meaning.

But meaning is the thing, isn’t it? We’re meaning-making machines. We can’t help it. Even when we try to escape it—through distraction, addiction, sheer exhaustion—it creeps back in. We tell ourselves stories to survive.

Here’s a story I tell myself: *One day, I’ll wake up and everything will make sense.* I’ll know exactly what to do, who to be, how to move through the world without second-guessing every step. But the older I get, the more I suspect that day will never come. And maybe that’s okay. Maybe the not-knowing is the point.

I read once that the ancient Greeks had two words for time: *chronos* and *kairos*. *Chronos* is the measurable, ticking-clock time—the kind that makes you panic when you realize you’re halfway through your life and still don’t have a 401(k). *Kairos* is the opportune moment, the right time, the pause between heartbeats where anything is possible.

Most of us spend our lives chasing *chronos*, trying to beat the clock, as if time were a race we could win. But *kairos* is where the magic happens. The spontaneous road trip. The conversation with a stranger that changes your perspective. The decision to stay when every instinct tells you to run.

I don’t know how to live in *kairos* more often. I don’t know how to quiet the noise of *chronos* long enough to hear it. But I’m trying.

A thousand words. I’ve used most of them now. I could fill the rest with advice—*drink more water, call your mother, be kind to yourself*—but what do I know? I’m just a person sitting in a room, typing into the void, hoping something resonates.

Maybe the point isn’t to have all the answers. Maybe the point is to keep asking questions, to stay curious, to hold the weight of not knowing and still show up tomorrow.

The cursor blinks. The coffee stain fades into the wood. The world keeps turning.

And so do I.
